title: Removal of Premarin highlights difficulty in accessing menopause treatment in Canada
summary: Earlier this month, Pfizer Canada announced it was discontinuing its hormone replacement therapy Premarin in Canada, but not in the U.S., citing “business reasons” — this despite an uptick in demand…

image.caption: Clinicians are raising concerns about access to menopause treatments in the wake of Pfizer ending the sale in Canada of a topical cream commonly prescribed to treat serious menopausal symptoms such as vaginal and vulvar irritation and atrophy, as well as increased risk of recurrent urinary tract inf

blocks.text: Finding menopause treatment that works for your body and doesn’t break the bank can be a long, complicated process — and many Canadians will soon be forced to start that process again.

Earlier this month, Pfizer Canada announced it was discontinuing its menopausal hormone therapy Premarin in Canada, but not in the U.S., citing "business reasons" — this despite an uptick in demand for such products.

Premarin’s topical cream formulation is one of only two vaginal estrogen creams approved by Health Canada and is widely covered under most provincial drug benefits. Now, clinicians are worried about access for their patients — the only other topical cream isn’t currently covered in B.C. and Ontario, Canada’s biggest provinces.

"To have [Premarin] removed actually reduces the access for all of those people — some of the most vulnerable people," said Jessica Bawden, a nurse practitioner and lead clinician in the Women's College Hospital menopause clinic in Toronto.
She noted that some of the symptoms treated by drugs like Premarin, such as the risk of recurrent urinary tract infections (UTIs), can have serious consequences if unaddressed.
"A UTI can be deadly, so this can be a preventative medicine to keep people out of hospital," she said. "Menopause is very normal, but suffering is not."

Jessica Bawden works at a menopause clinic in the Women's College Hospital in Toronto, and says she's concerned about access for patients who need to find an alternative for Premarin. (Craig Chivers/CBC)
Premarin comes in a vaginal cream and an oral tablet. The cream has been in short supply for months, but tablets are expected to remain available through mid-2027.

Premarin’s discontinuance comes as other menopausal treatments are becoming harder to find in Canada — a shortage in estradiol transdermal patches across the country is expected to persist into early 2027, according to Health Canada.
Vaginal irritation, pain, risk of recurrent UTIs
Dr. Sheila Wijayasinghe, a family doctor at Unity Health in Toronto, said it was a shock to find out Premarin — "one of the mainstays of our treatment options" — was being discontinued in Canada.

A number of vaginal estrogen products are approved in Canada to treat menopause symptoms, including oral tablets, vaginal suppositories and vaginal rings. The topical cream form of Premarin is commonly prescribed for those experiencing genitourinary syndrome, she said — a cluster of menopausal symptoms including vaginal irritation, vulvar irritation, pain during sexual intercourse and more frequent UTIs.

blocks.text: "Due to decreasing levels of estrogen, the tissues change. They can become more uncomfortable. We notice symptoms like urinary frequency, incontinence and an increased risk of bladder infections as well," Wijayasinghe said. "We can treat that very effectively with local vaginal estrogen."

Many of the more widely talked about menopause symptoms, like hot flashes and night sweats, get better over time. But genitourinary syndrome can worsen without appropriate treatment, and some form of it will affect the majority of people who go through menopause, she said.
Wijayasinghe also often prescribes Premarin cream to treat recurrent UTIs in seniors, "because it’s a very safe treatment option."
"I don't want to leave my patients without options," Wijayasinghe said. "I don’t want them to have to pay out of pocket if they're low-income … or they don't have private coverage."
Estragyn, made by Searchlight Pharma, is the only other topical cream vaginal estrogen product approved by Health Canada. (Craig Chivers/CBC)
B.C., Alberta expanding coverage options
The only other topical cream alternative approved by Health Canada is Estragyn, which is made by Searchlight Pharma.
It isn't a one-to-one equivalent of Premarin, as it uses the estrogen hormone estrone as its core ingredient, instead of conjugated estrogens.
But for patients who want a cream option — the only vaginal estrogen treatment that provides direct relief for external symptoms affecting the vulva — Estragyn is the sole alternative in Canada.

"[Vaginal suppositories] help more so with symptoms on the inside, but if you're having any symptoms on the outside, then it won't really help much for that," said Alexandra Hanna, a clinical pharmacist in the menopause clinic at Women’s College Hospital.

blocks.text: Estragyn costs around $70 a tube if you don’t have public or private coverage, she said. It’s covered by some provincial drug benefits, including Quebec’s and Manitoba’s, but not all.
Regina researcher focused on menopause and mental health
Under the Ontario Drug Benefit, those who are over 65 can access medications covered by OHIP; Premarin was one of those drugs. But Estragyn isn’t covered in Ontario.

When asked by CBC News if Ontario would consider adding Estragyn to the Ontario Drug Benefit, the province's Ministry of Health shared a list of three alternative vaginal estrogen products that Ontario already covers — none of which were topical creams.
Some provinces, however, are stepping up to expand coverage.

A spokesperson for Alberta’s health ministry said it has added Estragyn "as a temporary benefit" in response to Pfizer’s discontinuation of Premarin, and is working with the manufacturer to explore permanent coverage.

B.C.’s Ministry of Health, which covers Premarin cream through the National PharmaCare Plan, told CBC News it is "actively reviewing Estragyn as the replacement cream option following the discontinuation of Premarin."

Alexandra Hanna, a clinical pharmacist in the menopause clinic at Toronto's Women’s College Hospital, says patients should plan next steps with their doctors now instead of waiting for their Premarin supply to run out, to avoid gaps in their care. (Craig Chivers/CBC News)
Hanna hopes Ontario expands its coverage to include Estragyn, noting that many patients have been frustrated by Premarin’s discontinuation.
"For a lot of them, it takes a lot of trial and error to find something that works for them," she said.

There’s no generic form of Premarin cream, and switching to any new medication can be tough on the body. She advised that patients currently taking Premarin start discussing alternatives with their doctors now, instead of waiting.
Why did Pfizer discontinue the drug if demand is increasing?

It’s not uncommon for older drugs to be taken off the market, but Pfizer’s decision to discontinue Premarin in Canada, but not the U.S., has raised eyebrows, especially since its active ingredient — conjugated equine estrogens from pregnant mare urine — is produced in Brandon, Man.

Pfizer Canada told CBC News the decision reflected "a broader assessment of the long-term commercial sustainability" of supplying Premarin to Canada, adding they looked at "manufacturing and supply costs, the pricing and reimbursement environment, and the ability to maintain sustainable supply over the longer term."

“[Premarin] is a little bit more challenging than typical drugs to produce,” said Mina Tadrous, associate professor at the Lesley Dan Faculty of Pharmacy at the University of Toronto. “So there could be some truth in the higher cost and what those margins look like for them.”
As menopause products boom, many don't live up to the hype

He noted that global demand is up for menopause products amid increasing awareness in recent years. In the U.S. alone, monthly dispensing of menopause hormone therapy for women aged 40-74 years increased from two million in 2023 to 4.9 million by June 2026, a 141 per cent increase, according to a recent study published in JAMA.
This could have been a factor in Pfizer’s decision to withdraw it from the Canadian market despite increased demand here, too, Tadrous said.

"We've been for the last three years seeing a number of shortages for menopause-related therapies," Tadrous said. In the long term, the supply chain could catch up as companies enter to capitalize on demand, "but in the short term, you get this pain when you have these sudden increases in demand."

Pharmaceutical experts previously warned that a deal U.S. President Donald Trump made with pharmaceutical companies in September to lower drug prices in the U.S. could also impact Canada, suggesting companies might delay launching new drugs here to avoid creating a lower price comparison that could pull U.S. prices down further.
Trump’s push to cut pharma costs could drive up drug prices in Canada

In a blog post last Thursday, Canadian obstetrician-gynecologist Dr. Jen Gunter noted that a tube of Premarin cream in the U.S. sells for roughly $400-$500 US, 10 times more than what it costs in Canada.

blocks.text: Tadrous said it's tough to make the connection between the Premarin discontinuation and Trump's new most-favoured-nation (MFN) drug pricing, in part because of its age on the market.
But when products get pulled, Canada needs to find ways to stop patients from bearing the brunt, he said.
"I think what we need to do is start being more proactive. So when we know a drug is changing like this, can we go and find another source for it? Can we invest locally?" he said.
"How do we empower health-care providers and patients to be able to navigate this a little bit more easily?"
